Senator Joseph Rafferty, Chair Representative Kelly Murphy, Chair Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs c/o Legislative Information Office 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333

Re: Testimony in Opposition to LD 2204 - "An Act to Allow Schools to Expel Students for Committing Sexual Assault"

Dear Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs:

My name is Atlee Reilly and I am a Managing Attorney at Disability Rights Maine, Maine's protection and advocacy agency for individuals with disabilities. I am providing written testimony to follow up on my testimony at the public hearing in opposition to LD 2204 - "An Act to Allow Schools to Expel Students for Committing Sexual Assault".

I will not address the policy rationale for limiting the use of suspension and expulsion of pre-k to 5th grade students because that was addressed in detail by this Committee as recently as last session. Instead, I attach and incorporate prior testimony on the issue, including DRM's March 2025 testimony on LD 165 "An Act to Allow School Boards to Expel or Suspend Students Regardless of Grade Level". I also attach DRM's April 2021 testimony in support of LD 474 "An Act Regarding School Discipline for Maine's Youngest Students", which this proposal is clearly designed to roll back, as well as DRM's February 2020 testimony regarding LD 2016, which did not advance due to impacts of COVID-19.

As an initial matter, we want to make clear that schools can already expel students in Grade 6 and above for committing sexual assault. Maine law regarding expulsion is very broad and specifically includes "infractions of violence". See 20-A M.R.S. � 1001(9)(B). This would of course include sexual assault. The only children who are protected from expulsion under current

law are students in Grade 5 and below. Or, put another way, the Students protected from expulsion under current law are students who are generally 5-10 years old. So those are the children you should keep in mind when thinking about this bill. They are the only ones it will impact in any significant way.
In addition to establishing what amounts to a legal presumption for the expulsion of young children determined (by a school administrator) to have committed sexual assault as defined in Maine criminal statute, LD 2204 would also require the creation of policies to refer these children to an "appropriate law enforcement agency". But in 2025, through L.D. 1849, Maine joined many other jurisdictions by enacting a minimum age for juvenile court jurisdiction. The age Maine set is 11. See: 15 M.R.S. � 3003 (defining juvenile for purposes of the juvenile code and juvenile court jurisdiction as "A person who has attained 11 years of age but had not attained 18 years of age at the time the person allegedly committed any juvenile crime..."). There are many reasons for this, including that a 5,6,7,8,9, or 10 year old would be almost certainly not be deemed competent to stand trial.
It is concerning that school principals and school boards would be tasked with applying a criminal statute, especially this one, to children ages 5-10. The existing statutory language referenced in the bill, Title 17-A Chapter 11, covers a wide range of behaviors. The way this is written means that the same disciplinary measure would be required for all students for any form of sexual assault - from gross sexual assault to unlawful sexual touching. The crimes under this chapter range from felony to misdemeanor. Here, children who exhibit any of the conduct described in the chapter would be subject to the same harsh outcome and loss of access to education. The outcome for gross sexual assault (Class A felony) is the same as that of touching of buttocks over clothing (Class D misdemeanor assuming intent criteria met).
Addressing problem sexual behavior in schools is an extremely important goal. But expelling students as young as 5 is not the appropriate response. While we think that the Committee should reject this proposal, if the Committee is inclined to consider it, it should first seek input from experts in problem sexual behavior of children as well as experts in juvenile law who can discuss the implications of using this particular criminal statute in the context of school discipline for very young children. The Committee should also seek input from individuals and organizations with expertise in addressing problem sexual behavior in schools if it intends to legislate in this space, to ensure that the most effective methods are used and to avoid unintended consequences. In addition, individuals with expertise in the already existing obligations of schools under Title IX could also help shed light on the fact that schools already have a responsibility to take effective action to prevent and/or appropriately respond to and address the harms from problem sexual behavior and other forms of sexual harassment in schools.1

Additional information maintained by USDOE is available here: https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/civil-rights-laws/title-ixand-sex-discrimination/sex-discrimination-overview-of-law.

With regard to the proposal to require the expulsion and referral to law enforcement of pre-K to 5th grade students, we submit this is not the right approach. This population is unique as indicated in a guide titled Know Your Child's Rights (K-5): K-5 Sexual Harassment and Assault from Equal Rights Advocates:
In the context of peer-on-peer sexual harassment or assault, a key difference at the K-5 level is the purpose of the discipline or response. Given the likely young age of the child exhibiting the problematic behavior, the school's focus should center on taking a caring and deliberate stance toward both protecting the victim and addressing the harmer's behavior. In these instances, the school is positioned to both facilitate the harmer's learning of proper behavior and explore whether any harm or other alarming stressors are instigating the behavior. Early intervention helps to ensure that the school sufficiently addresses improper behavior before it escalates and has the power to prevent further harm to your child, the harmer's current classmates, and future peers as the child ages. Ideally, intervening when the harmer is so young will also help them avoid future negative life consequences from escalating harmful behavior.2
In our view, the primary impact of this bill will be that many children, ages 5-10, will be identified by their schools as having committed a sexual assault as defined in Maine's criminal code when they could not even be charged with that crime. Schools who may not have the resources to address the needs of a child engaging in problem sexual behavior or who may otherwise want to rid themselves of a student, will be incentivized to label the behavior of very young children as criminal sexual conduct in order to expel them as this law would require.
We would be happy to provide additional information if needed. And we urge you to vote ought not to pass on LD 2204.
Respectfully Submitted,
Atlee Reilly Managing Attorney Disability Rights Maine

My name is Atlee Reilly and I am a managing attorney at Disability Rights Maine, Maine's protection and advocacy agency for people with disabilities, testifying in support of LD 474 - "An Act Regarding School Discipline for Maine's Youngest Students". LD 474 would limit the use of out of school suspensions and expulsions for students in grade 5 and below. LD 474 would also ensure that any student in Maine facing an expulsion from school be provided information about how to obtain legal representation.1 And LD 474 would end the counterproductive practice of withholding recess from elementary school students as a form of punishment.2

Simply put, suspensions are harmful and do not make schools safer.3 There is no evidence that the use of suspensions improves school safety and climate or student behavior, and in fact, there is evidence that elementary school suspensions are the best predictor of suspensions later in school.4 School attendance is, not surprisingly, linked to school achievement. One recent analysis found that fourth grade students who missed three or more days of school had reading scores more than a full grade level below their peers.5 Recent research indicates students may have lower academic achievement just by attending schools with high suspension rates, even if they themselves are not suspended.6 Disciplinary removals also increase the risk of a range of educational, economic, and social problems, including dropout and involvement with the juvenile justice system.7 And students of color and students with disabilities are disproportionately subjected to and impacted by suspensions and other removals.8 Suspensions, especially for younger children, also increase the stress on families that are already struggling. Introducing LD 2204, "An Act to Allow Schools to Expel Students for Committing Sexual Assault"
Presented before the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs February 26, 2026
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and Members of the Committee on Education and Cultural
Affairs, my name is Craig Hickman. I have the honor and privilege of representing the good people of
Senate District 14, comprised of the municipalities of Chelsea, Farmingdale, Gardiner, Hallowell,
Manchester, Monmouth, Pittston, Randolph, Readfield, Wayne, West Gardiner and Winthrop.
Late last year, I was contacted by a constituent of mine who informed me that her 6-year-old daughter who is attending Kindergarten had repeatedly been sexually assaulted by one of her classmates, also 6
years old. This had happened several times.
When my constituent and the father of her child were informed of these assaults and inquired as to why
this student had not been removed from the school, they were frustrated to leam from the superintendent
that current State statute -- specifically, Title 20-A �l001 (9) -- prevents this student from being expelled from the school. When my office contacted the superintendent of the school, it was confirmed
that the school received legal advice that expelling the student would be extremely difficult under current state statute and could invite litigation.
Therefore, to ensure unimaginable incidents like this can be properly dealt with under our statutory landscape, this bill amends current law to require that school boards adopt a policy for expelling a student
enrolled in any grade who is determined to have committed sexual assault on school grounds or other school property. This bill also requires that any student who is determined to have committed sexual
assault must be expelled from school for a period of not less than one year, unless a school board authorized the superintendent to modify in writing the requirement for expulsion of a student on a case-
by-case basis.
The proposed language mirrors language in current statute regarding disciplining students who bring
firearms to school.
Thank you for your time and consideration on this matter. I would be happy to answer any questions the
committee may have.

TESTIMONY NEITHER FOR NOR AGAINST

AN ACT TO ALLOW SCHOOLS TO EXPEL STUDENTS FOR COMMITTING SEXUAL ASSAULT

February 26, 2026

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I
am Eric Waddell, Executive Director for Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the
legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and Maine School Superintendents
Association neither for nor against L.D. 2204. We appreciate the serious nature of the conduct this bill seeks
to address and the need to ensure a safe enviromnent for all students.

20-A M.R.S.A. �1001(9) outlines situations that could prompt expulsion, including deliberate disobedience, infractions of violence, and possession of weapons or drugs "if found necessary for the peace and usefulness of the school." The statute also prohibits expulsion of students enrolled in grades pre-K through five, with the only exception being for violations of the federal Gun-Free Schools Act. This provision mandates a one-year
expulsion for any student who brings a firearm to school, regardless of grade level but provides for the same
flexibility this bill does, which authorizes the superintendent to modify in writing the requirement for expulsion of a student on a case-by-case basis.

L.D. 2204 would create a new mandate for school boards to also adopt policies to expel students of any grade who are found to have committed sexual assault "on school grounds or other school property and for referring
the matter to the appropriate local law enforcement agency."
We appreciate the language in the bill that provides that a school board "may authorize the superintendent to
modzjy in writing the requirement for expulsion of a student on a case-by-case basis. " This flexibility is
essential. It allows school leaders, who are closest to the situation, to make decisions based on the specific
facts of an incident, the age and developmental maturity of the student, and any other related circumstances. This provision ensures that expulsion is not an automatic mandate but a measure of last resort.

It is important to note that school boards already have the authority to expel a student for sexual assault, as

well as the authority not to expel. This bill would not appear to change that authority but instead add more

specificity in statute.

' I

We do have some concerns that this mandate would apply to every child - regardless of grade level.
Developmental and psychological research makes clear that elementary-aged children are still building the cognitive and emotional skills needed to fully understand the consequences of their actions. Their brains are
developing, and they are learning how to manage behavior and navigate complex social situations. Expelling a
young child removes the opportunity for the district to design and implement targeted interventions that address the root causes of the behavior and prevent it from recurring. This is a critical time to provide

Eric F. Waddell MSBA Executive Direclor

Eileen E. King MSSA Executive Director
,

guidance, instruction, and support----not to remove children from the very systems designed to help them grow and succeed.
Expulsion, as the most severe form of school discipline, can have a profoundly negative and lasting impact on a young child's educational trajectory and social-emotional development.
Other interventions--such as counseling, restorative justice practices, and intensive behavioral support--are often more effective in addressing the root causes of behavior and promoting a safe and positive school
climate for everyone. Considering all of these factors, we urge your committee to amend this bill to allow for
expulsions only for students in 6*" grade or older.
In addition, the definition of sexual assault in L.D. 2204 includes any actions "as described in Title I 7-A, chapter 11." This is a broad definition and could conceivably encompass a widearray of circumstances. Administrators and board members would likely need additional training to understand the full extent of this language and what situations it does - and does not -- apply to.
Our Associations also would suggest that you strike Part C of the bill, which would allow a principal to
"suspend" a student "immediately for good cause." Under Title IX, schools are required to maintain a presumption of innocence until the full investigation is completed. L.D. 2204 would appear to conflict with Title IX regulations and could lead to confusion among school districts.
Thank you for your time and consideration -- I am happy to answer any questions you may have.

Testimony of Howard Tuttle, Superintendent of RSU 12 In Support of LD 2204, "An Act to Allow Schools to Expel Students for Committing Sexual Assault" Before the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Howard Tuttle, and I am the Superintendent of RSU 12. I am testifying today to offer my support for LD 2204. As a Superintendent, I believe that local school boards need more flexibility and options regarding the placement of students in grades 5 and below who have committed serious violations of board policy. The current Maine statute, Title 20-A �1001(9), makes it very difficult for school districts to remove students from the school setting, even in cases of egregious behavior. This bill fills a critical need by giving school boards a tool to address incidents of sexual assault through an expulsion policy. LD 2204 states that school boards must adopt a policy regarding the expulsion of any student, of any grade level, who is found to have committed sexual assault on school grounds. The expulsion period must be at least one year, but the Superintendent may, in writing, waive this on a case-by-case basis. Notably, this legislation also states that school boards have the authority to continue providing educational services to an expelled student in an alternative setting, provided that the safety of the victim and the school community is maintained and that the offender is not left entirely without educational support. Although I am in full support of the flexibility that this bill provides in the case of sexual assault, I would like to ask the Committee to consider broadening the scope of this legislation. School boards should have the same flexibility and options available to them for students in grades 5 and below who display serious and dangerous behavioral issues. By giving school boards more flexibility to deal with a variety of high-risk behaviors, it would be possible to ensure that all students have a safe and supportive learning environment. Thank you for your time and consideration of this issue.

Testimony Neither For Nor Against LD 2204: An Act to Allow Schools to Expel Students for Committing Sexual Assault Jesse Hargrove, President, Maine Education Association Before The Education and Cultural Affairs committee
February 25th, 2026
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and other members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee,
My name is Jesse Hargrove, I am a high school social studies teacher on leave to serve as Maine Education Association President. The MEA represents nearly 24,000 educators. Our members include teachers and other educators in nearly every public school in the state, full-time faculty and other professional and support staff in both the University of Maine and Community College systems, and thousands of retired educators.
I offer this testimony today on behalf of the MEA Neither For Nor Against LD 2204, An Act to Allow Schools to Expel Students for Committing Sexual Assault.
The Maine Education Association emphatically believes schools should be safe places for students to learn free of sexual assault and harassment. However this bill presents a number of concerns without offering remedy. First, the bill explicitly provides expulsion to students of all grades and ages, particularly those in grade 5 or below. The MEA has consistently opposed expulsion for students in elementary grade levels, particularly grade five and under. These children are in the most formative years. Students who are disciplined with expulsion are at an increased risk for dropping out of school and future involvement with the juvenile justice system. About 40 % of students with a history of juvenile incarceration are re-incarcerated as adults. This has become known as the "School to Prison Pipeline".i Furthermore, expulsions are disproportionately applied to students who identify as Black, American Indian/Alaskan Native, Students with Disabilities particularly attention disorders, intellectual disabilities, or emotional disturbances, and those who identify as LGBTQ+.ii

Time away from school hurts kids and sets them up for long-term struggles with the law and loss of economic opportunity. The National Sexual Violence Resource Council (NSVRC) suggests that people who commit sexual abuse are portrayed as "monsters" making it more challenging to perceive the risks and warning signs. Common factors of people committing sexual abuse a family history of conflict or violence; a childhood history of physical, sexual, or emotional abuse; poverty; lack of institutional support; and exposure to explicit material. Children with these backgrounds need more support from their schools and communities. Furthermore, the NSVRC also suggests that youth who abuse "often do not reoffend, and they are generally very receptive to treatment."iii
We recognize the intent of the bill is to make schools safer for students by reducing risks of sexual assault. It neglects to address underlying causes or risk factors, nor does it establish systemic supports for youth who have committed sexual assault. These children and young people, who are likely from under-resourced environments and coping with their own traumatic experiences, will be further alienated, and subject to further economic and legal challenges. We believe there are other more supportive ways to invest in our schools and students to support children with risk factors to more effectively prevent sexual assault. Furthermore, we see this bill as recognition of need for Behavioral and Mental Services called for in LD 858 and would recommend further investment in these preventative measures.
